questions.stem: A 43-year-old woman traveled to West Africa for a year-long research project. A few weeks into her trip she began to notice strange dreams followed by a paranoid feeling of people following her.
questions.lead_in: What prophylactic agent is most likely to be responsible?
questions.explanation: Mefloquine A variety of neuropsychiatric side effects of mefloquine are well described. In particular, strange dreams and sensations of paranoia are among the most frequent.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 1 Q8

questions.stem: A 32-year-old woman sought travel advice for a 1-week trip to Zambia. Her departure date was in 1 month. She was 16-weeks pregnant. She intended to visit friends and relatives. She was given advice regarding mosquito bite avoidance.
questions.lead_in: What is the most appropriate malaria chemoprophylaxis?

options.text: Medical prophylaxis contraindicated due to pregnancy

questions.explanation: Mefloquine Pregnancy is a risk factor for severe disease in malaria, and pregnant women are advised to avoid travel to malarious areas. However, if travel cannot be avoided, then prophylaxis for malaria should be offered to all patients traveling to areas at risk. Although chloroquine is safe in all trimesters of pregnancy, resistance in Plasmodium falciparum is widespread, and mefloquine is the only other medication shown to be safe for use during pregnancy and that remains active in most areas. Doxycycline and atovaquone–proguanil should not be used in pregnancy.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 2 Q43

questions.stem: A 29-year-old woman attended for pretravel advice. She was planning a 1-week trip to Haiti. She was 25 weeks pregnant, and it was her first pregnancy.
questions.lead_in: What is the most appropriate malaria prophylaxis?
questions.explanation: Chloroquine Malaria prophylaxis is indicated as Haiti is considered at moderate risk for acquisition of malaria. Although Plasmodium falciparum accounts for almost all cases of malaria in Haiti, resistance is exceedingly rare. In addition, the patient is pregnant, and the only medication that is considered safe from the above list is chloroquine. Atovaquone–proguanil, artemether–lumefantrine, and doxycycline are contraindicated regardless of the trimester. Mosquito bite avoidance is extremely important, and suitable precautions must be discussed. She should also be advised that national recommendations (both CDC and the PHE Advisory Committee on Malaria Prevention) are that pregnant women should avoid all nonessential travel to malarious areas due to the increased risk of severe malaria and death or serious adverse outcomes such as stillbirth and miscarriage.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 4 Q33

questions.stem: A 27-year-old woman attended clinic for pretravel counseling. She was 18 weeks pregnant. She was planning a 2-week holiday to Kenya to visit her husband. It was her first pregnancy and had been uneventful to date. She was taking prenatal vitamins and was allergic to penicillin (rash only). She was given advice on mosquito bite avoidance and insect repellent.
questions.lead_in: What would be the most appropriate malaria chemo prophylaxis?
questions.explanation: Mefloquine Mefloquine is the drug of choice for prophylaxis in the setting of pregnancy. Clindamycin is not an adequate drug for malaria chemoprophylaxis. Hydroxychloroquine and doxycycline should not be used during pregnancy due to teratogenic effects. Atovaquone–proguanil has emerging data for use during pregnancy, but mefloquine remains the drug of choice for chemoprophylaxis during pregnancy. If travel is essential, the risk of any prophylactic drug in pregnancy has to be weighed against the risk of contracting malaria. However, do not forget that pregnant women should be advised to avoid traveling to malarial areas; pregnant women are at higher risk of severe malaria, and malaria increases the risk of adverse fetal outcomes, including premature birth and stillbirth.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 5 Q31

questions.question: A Canadian traveller has severe malaria: Hb 65 g/L, SaO2 85%, confused with GCS 9, and Plasmodium falciparum parasitemia of 6%.
questions.question_raw: 17.  Severe malaria in Canadian traveller.  Has Hb 65. Sao2 of 85%. Confused and GCS 9. Falciparum parasitemia of 6%.

parts.text: What criteria does he have for severe disease?
What is the histopathologic feature of cerebral malaria?
What are four other criteria for severe disease?
What is the treatment?

parts_raw.text: A.  What criteria does he have for severe disease?
B.  What is the histopathologic feature of cerebral malaria?
C.  What are four other criteria for severe disease?
D.  What is the treatment?

questions.model_answer:
a) Criteria met in this nonimmune traveller: (1) Cerebral malaria — impaired consciousness (GCS 9); (2) Respiratory distress/hypoxia — SaO2 85%; (3) Severe anaemia — Hb 65 g/L; (4) Hyperparasitaemia — P. falciparum 6% (any parasitaemia is dangerous in a nonimmune host).
b) Sequestration (cytoadherence) of P. falciparum–infected erythrocytes in the cerebral microvasculature; classically accompanied by ring haemorrhages.
c) Four other criteria: (1) prostration; (2) hypoglycaemia; (3) jaundice/icterus; (4) renal insufficiency (also shock, hemoglobinuria, metabolic acidosis, repetitive vomiting, hyperpyrexia).
d) IV artesunate 2.4 mg/kg at 0, 12, 24 and 48 h (preferred; obtained in Canada through the Canadian Malaria Network), followed by a full oral course (e.g., atovaquone-proguanil) once able to take PO; parenteral quinine is the alternative.
questions.beyond_mandell: Ring haemorrhages as the classic cerebral-malaria neuropathology is standard WHO/pathology teaching; the text emphasizes sequestration/cytoadherence.

cohort_answer.text:
Parasetemia >5% in non-immune for >5yo; Hb <70; ARDS; Impaired conciousness
Sequestration of infected RBCs in brain microvasculature, ring haemorrhages
IV artesunate for at least 24 hours then complete therapy with a course of atovaquone-proguanil

questions.question: A patient travelled to India and Cambodia while taking mefloquine prophylaxis and returns to Canada with symptoms of severe malaria and a positive rapid test.
questions.question_raw: Patient who traveled to India and Cambodia. Malaria prophylaxis with Mefloquine. Sx severe malaria and positive rapid test when returning to Canada.

parts.text: Which Plasmodium species is most likely involved?
Explain why.
What is the place of acquisition?
Name two treatments (first and second line).
Explain why first-line treatment is better.
How would you monitor the potential emergence of resistance to first-line treatment?

parts_raw.text: Which Plasmodium species is most likely involved?
Explain why?
What is the place of acquisition?
Name two treatments (first and second line)
Explain why first-line treatment is better
How to monitor the potential emergence of resistance to first-line treatment?

questions.model_answer:
a) Plasmodium falciparum.
b) Both India and Cambodia transmit falciparum and vivax, but P. falciparum is the species that characteristically causes severe malaria; breakthrough of severe disease despite mefloquine prophylaxis fits mefloquine-resistant P. falciparum.
c) Cambodia (Greater Mekong subregion of Southeast Asia), a region of documented mefloquine resistance.
d) First-line: IV artesunate. Second-line: IV quinine (or quinidine) plus doxycycline/clindamycin.
e) Artesunate clears parasitaemia faster and reduced mortality by ~22-35% versus quinine in randomized trials; it is safer and better tolerated, with less cardiotoxicity and hypoglycaemia and no need for continuous ECG monitoring.
f) Serial blood smears to measure parasite clearance (clearance half-life) — delayed clearance signals emerging artemisinin resistance (associated with K13 propeller mutations).

cohort_answer.text:
Species: P. falciparum
Why: Falciparum & vivax sp are found in both countries but falciparum is the only one that typically causes severe malaria. Known mefloquine resistance in Cambodia.
Place of acquisition: Cambodia (has areas of Mefloquine resistance)
Treatments: Parentral Artesunate; Parentral Quinine + clinda
Why first-line better: Rapid activity, clears parasitemia faster; Activity against all erythrocytic stages of the parasite; Minimal resistance; Very well tolerated, less adverse effects compared to quinine (eg hypoglycaemia); Easy to administer; No dose adjustment for organ impairment; No significant drug interactions; Does not require cardiac monitoring. Disadvantages: Short half life <2hrs therefore can relapse if not given an oral course as step down; Can cause delayed haemolysis (weekly CBCs x 4 weeks)
Monitoring resistance: Repeat blood smears to monitor clearance of parasitemia – if delayed, may have resistance

questions.question: A healthy man is traveling to Honduras (chloroquine-sensitive) and requires malaria prophylaxis.
questions.question_raw: A healthy man is traveling to Honduras (chloroquine sensitive) and requires malaria prophylaxis.

parts.text: Name 4 options for malaria prophylaxis, and indicate when to start and when to stop each (table: prophylactic agent, start, stop).

parts_raw.text: Name 4 options for malaria prophylaxis, and indicate when to start and to stop for each (table: Prophylactic agent, start, stop)

questions.model_answer:
a) Four appropriate regimens (Honduras is chloroquine-sensitive, so all four classes are options):
(1) Atovaquone-proguanil (Malarone) 250/100 mg PO daily - start 1-2 days before travel; continue daily during travel; stop 7 days after leaving the endemic area (short post-travel course because it also has causal/liver-stage activity).
(2) Doxycycline 100 mg PO daily - start 1-2 days before travel; continue daily during travel; stop 4 weeks after leaving.
(3) Mefloquine 250 mg salt PO weekly - start 1-2 weeks before travel (ideally 2-3 weeks to confirm tolerance); continue weekly during travel; stop 4 weeks after leaving.
(4) Chloroquine 500 mg salt PO weekly - start 1-2 weeks before travel; continue weekly during travel; stop 4 weeks after leaving.
questions.beyond_mandell: Start/stop schedules follow CDC Yellow Book / PHAC CATMAT traveler guidance; the chapter confirms the agents and dosing frequency but does not tabulate prophylaxis timing.

questions.question: Give examples of drugs or drug classes that prolong the QT interval, using each class only once.
questions.question_raw: In the following examples, please give examples of drugs or drug classes that prolong QT (You can only use the same class once)

parts.text: Two antibacterials.
One antiviral.
One antiparasitic.
One antimycobacterial.

parts_raw.text: 2 antibacterial
1 antiviral
1 antiparasitic
1 antimycobacterial

questions.model_answer:
a) (1) Macrolides (erythromycin, clarithromycin, azithromycin) — associated with QT prolongation and torsades de pointes, especially with CYP3A4 inhibitors or other QT-prolonging drugs; (2) Fluoroquinolones (moxifloxacin, levofloxacin).
b) One antiviral: an HIV protease inhibitor (e.g., saquinavir, usually ritonavir-boosted).
c) One antiparasitic: an antimalarial such as chloroquine/hydroxychloroquine or quinine (pentamidine also acceptable).
d) One antimycobacterial: bedaquiline (clofazimine and delamanid also prolong QT).
questions.beyond_mandell: Only the macrolide (and fluoroquinolone interaction) QT risk is in this chapter; the antiviral, antiparasitic, and antimycobacterial examples rest on general pharmacology/product labelling and QT-drug lists (e.g., CredibleMeds).

questions.question: A 24-year-old with recent travel to Malawi was treated 10 days ago there for uncomplicated P. falciparum malaria with artemether-lumefantrine for 3 days and now feels well.
questions.question_raw: 24yo with recent travel to Malawi, reports he was treated 10 days ago there for uncomplicated P. falciparum malaria with artemisinin-lumefantrine x 3 days. Feeling well.

parts.text: The RDT is positive for P. falciparum (no smear given). Give 4 reasons for this result.
Thick and thin smear shows only gametocytes for P. falciparum, bloodwork otherwise normal apart from anemia. Would you treat again, and give a reason? No travel planned in the next year.
Give two regimens for treating uncomplicated falciparum malaria available in Canada.

parts_raw.text: RDT is positive for P falciparum (no smear given). Give 4 reasons for this result.
Thick and thin smear shows only gametocytes for P falciparum, B/W otherwise normal apart from anemia. Would you treat again and give a reason. No travel planned in the next year.
Give two regimens for treating uncomplicated falciparum malaria available in Canada

questions.model_answer:
a) (1) Persistent HRP-2 antigenaemia (RDT stays positive up to ~28 days after successful treatment); (2) Circulating gametocytes not cleared by artemether-lumefantrine; (3) Recrudescence/treatment failure with residual asexual parasites; (4) Re-infection with a new falciparum infection.
b) No — only gametocytes are present (no asexual parasites) in a well patient, representing residual gametocytaemia after successful cure; gametocytes are non-pathogenic and resolve spontaneously. With no onward travel and no local transmission, re-treatment is not indicated (transmission-blocking single-dose primaquine is unnecessary here).
c) Two Canadian regimens for uncomplicated falciparum: (1) atovaquone-proguanil (Malarone) x3 days; (2) artemether-lumefantrine (Coartem) [alternative: quinine plus doxycycline].
questions.beyond_mandell: Gametocyte persistence after ACT and single-dose primaquine for transmission-blocking reflect WHO/CDC guidance beyond this chapter.

questions.question: A traveler returning from India via Cambodia (stayed several days, no clear timeline given) had been adherent to mefloquine prophylaxis and now presents 7 days post-return with fevers and a positive malaria rapid diagnostic test.
questions.question_raw: Travel returning from India via Cambodia (stayed there several days – no clear timeline given during trip) had been on mefloquine prophylaxis and adherent, now 7 days post return with fevers and + malaria RDT.

parts.text: What is the pathogen and where was it acquired?
Recommended treatment and one alternative.
What are the advantages to this regimen?
What should you monitor for?

parts_raw.text: a) what is pathogen and where was it acquired?
b) Recommended treatment and 1 alternative
c) What are the advantages to this regimen
d) What should you monitor for?

questions.model_answer:
a) Mefloquine-resistant Plasmodium falciparum, acquired in Cambodia. Mefloquine is effective for infections acquired in India but not in Southeast Asia (Thailand, Myanmar, southern China, Cambodia, Laos, Vietnam), where mefloquine resistance is established; breakthrough on adherent prophylaxis therefore points to a Cambodian-acquired resistant strain.
b) Assuming uncomplicated disease: atovaquone-proguanil (Malarone) 4 adult tablets daily x3 days OR artemether-lumefantrine (Coartem). Alternative: quinine sulfate plus doxycycline. A drug taken as prophylaxis (mefloquine) is not used for treatment. If severe: IV artesunate.
c) (1) Rapid parasite/fever clearance (artemisinins act within 24-36 h). (2) High efficacy against multidrug-resistant parasites with low resistance rates. (3) Well tolerated with oral dosing and few contraindications (atovaquone-proguanil); artesunate reduces mortality 22-35% vs quinine in severe disease.
d) Serial (daily) blood smears for parasite density until negative - failure of parasitemia to fall or recrudescence suggests resistance. Monitor for features of severe malaria (glucose, creatinine, lactate, Hb). If IV artesunate is used, check hemoglobin around day 14 for delayed post-artesunate hemolysis.

cohort_answer.text:
Mefloquine-resistant P falciparum - Cambodia. (P vivax - Africa/Asia/South Pacific/Central-South America, possible but mefloquine resistance low unless Papua New Guinea; P ovale unlikely, endemic W Africa rarely SE Asia; P malariae exists in SEA but mefloquine sensitive/infrequent). RDTs: HRP2 targets P falciparum only, LDH and Aldolase pan-plasmodium
(Assuming NOT severe) Oral Artemisinin combination therapy (ACT); Malarone; Quinine + Clinda/Doxy. If severe: artesunate 2.4mg/kg 0,12,24,48hr + clindamycin or doxycycline or malarone; Alternative: Quinine 5.8mg/kg PLUS malarone/doxy/clinda
Mortality benefit with artesunate; oral/rectal options; dual treatment decreases treatment failure; less side effects; quicker drop in malaria load, kills all stages; low resistance rates
Parasite density typically daily until negative; if artesunate used, monitor weekly CBC for delayed hemolysis (up to 4 weeks after). Artesunate preferred: IV form, mortality benefit. Resistance suspected if recrudescence/parasite density does not drop
